content: True filarial hydrocele is believed to develop following the death of adult filarial worms, whereas a chylocele results from the accumulation of fluid due to the rupture of lymphatic vessels within the scrotal cavity. A classification system for hydrocele has been proposed and adopted by an expert consultation panel to standardize management procedures and facilitate international comparisons. Many individuals living in areas endemic to lymphatic filariasis (LF) may remain asymptomatic but exhibit subclinical lymphatic abnormalities, such as vessel dilation, detectable through ultrasonography or lymphoscintigraphy. Additionally, microscopic hematuria associated with microfilariae can be observed in otherwise asymptomatic individuals. Other clinical manifestations of LF include chyluria, hematochyluria, and tropical pulmonary eosinophilia (TPE). Chyluria is characterized by the presence of chyle in the urine, giving it a milky appearance, and occurs due to the rupture of dilated lymphatic vessels into the urinary system. Hematochyluria involves the presence of blood in the urine. TPE is an immunologic hypersensitivity reaction to microfilariae in the lungs, presenting with symptoms such as cough, fever, marked eosinophilia, elevated serum immunoglobulin E levels, and positive antifilarial antibodies. The socioeconomic burden of LF is significant, as conditions like lymphedema and hydrocele lead to permanent disability, disfigurement, and associated psychosocial and economic consequences. The direct costs of managing acute and chronic manifestations are a financial strain on both patients and healthcare systems. For example, hydrocele surgery costs range from $5 to $60 depending on the country and source of care, while indirect losses due to reduced productivity severely impact local and national economies. In India, acute dermatolymphangioadenitis (ADL) is estimated to cause annual losses of $60–85 million, and in the Philippines, $38 million per year. Chronic manifestations often force patients to stop working or take on less productive jobs, further exacerbating economic challenges. LF also imposes a heavy social burden, as chronic complications are often stigmatized, preventing patients from fulfilling societal roles or leading emotionally fulfilling lives. For men, genital damage causes physical limitations and social stigmatization, while women with lymphedema or elephantiasis face shame and taboos, particularly when their lower limbs or genitals are enlarged. This stigma can make marriage, a critical source of security in many cultures, unattainable. Such individuals are at increased risk of depression and poor mental health. LF affects not only the patient but also their families, especially if the patient is the primary income earner. The World Health Organization (WHO) International Classification of Functioning, Disability, and Health provides a framework for understanding the biological, individual, and social aspects of health. In the context of LF, individuals with clinical manifestations experience disability when these conditions interfere with daily life or professional activities. For example, men with small hydroceles may not face difficulties riding a bicycle, but larger hydroceles can impede such activities. Social stigma and limited access to services further restrict participation in societal and professional roles. The management of LF-related morbidity and disability is essential to alleviate suffering and improve quality of life. Primary prevention involves mass drug administration (MDA) to reduce LF transmission and prevent new infections. Secondary and tertiary prevention focuses on providing care for infected individuals, including hygiene, skin and wound care, elevation, exercises, and hydrocele surgery. The Global Programme to Eliminate Lymphatic Filariasis (GPELF) aims to stop LF transmission through MDA and alleviate suffering through morbidity management and disability prevention (MMDP). MDA involves annual administration of antifilarial drugs, such as albendazole, diethylcarbamazine, and ivermectin, to at-risk populations for at least five years. This approach reduces transmission rates, prevents disease progression, and improves economic productivity. MMDP focuses on managing acute attacks, lymphedema, and hydrocele, as well as providing access to essential care packages. Hygiene is the cornerstone of lymphedema management, reducing the incidence of acute attacks and preventing disease progression. Daily washing with soap and clean water, careful drying, and wound care are critical. Elevation and regular low-intensity exercises promote lymphatic flow, while wearing comfortable shoes protects against injury. Hydrocele is effectively treated through surgery, which improves men’s economic situations, community participation, and quality of life. The integration of LF management into broader healthcare systems and other disease control programs, such as those for diabetes, leprosy, and neglected tropical diseases, enhances resource efficiency and sustainability. Training healthcare workers and community members to care for individuals with chronic disabling conditions is vital. Addressing stigma, promoting positive attitudes, and providing vocational training and psychological support are essential components of comprehensive care. Ultimately, the goal of MMDP is to provide every person with LF a better, more productive life and enable equal participation in society. By 2030, national programs aim to achieve full geographic coverage of basic care for all individuals with LF-related conditions. This aligns with the principles of universal health coverage, ensuring equitable access to high-quality health services without financial hardship.
